opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest mistake people make is treating intelligence as one number, as if a model that does well on a hard math benchmark must be generally smarter across the board. Intelligence is much more jagged than that, especially for these systems.

It helps to borrow from the psychometrics literature on human cognition and break intelligence into components. There's general knowledge, reading and writing, mathematical ability, and on-the-spot reasoning, meaning solving novel problems you haven't seen before. There's working memory, and then long-term memory, which splits into two things: storing new information and retrieving it reliably. There's visual processing, auditory processing, and speed. When you look at models along those axes, the profile is very uneven. They're superhuman on knowledge and quite strong on reading, writing, and a lot of math. But they can be surprisingly weak at continual learning, at actually storing new experiences and building on them over days or weeks. Some aspects of visual reasoning and fluid reasoning on truly novel problems are also still shaky.

So when I see a benchmark result, my first question is which of these capacities it's actually measuring. A lot of benchmarks mostly load on knowledge and crystallized skill. Those have been saturating quickly, and it's easy to read that as rapid progress toward general intelligence. Progress there is real, but it doesn't tell you much about the bottleneck dimensions. A system can score extremely well on graduate-level exam questions and still fail to remember what you told it last Tuesday or to learn a new workflow on the job.

That matters for forecasting and for safety. If you collapse everything into one score, you'll be surprised in both directions. You'll overestimate what models can do autonomously in the real world, because the weak links like memory and long-horizon reliability bottleneck economically useful work. And you'll underestimate how fast things could change once those specific gaps close, because the other capabilities are already sitting there at a very high level. A system that's superhuman in knowledge and gets competent continual learning could see a big discontinuity in practical capability.

So I'd encourage people to think of benchmark performance as a profile, not a ranking. Look for the weakest dimensions, because that's often where the real story is.

r001.rationale: The response says models can be strong in math yet still fail at memory and learning workflows, which it describes as bottlenecks for useful real-world work.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues that intelligence is not one number and recommends treating benchmark performance as a profile across dimensions.

r003.rationale: It discusses visual processing, but does not identify image classification as a facet of crystallized intelligence.

r004.rationale: It explains how strong benchmark results can coexist with limited useful work, but describes scoring “extremely well,” not perfect benchmark performance.

r005.rationale: It does not propose human-level performance across cognitive dimensions as a conception of AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that "intelligence" as a single number is a pretty lossy summary, and benchmarks tend to get interpreted as if they're measuring that one number when they're really measuring one slice of it. When we built the "Definition of AGI" framework, we borrowed from the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model from psychometrics, which is the most empirically validated theory of human cognitive abilities we have. It breaks intelligence into a set of broad abilities: things like general knowledge, reading and writing, mathematical reasoning, on-the-spot reasoning, working memory, long-term memory storage and retrieval, visual processing, auditory processing, and speed.

And once you adopt that lens, the current frontier models look very jagged. On knowledge and reading and writing, they're basically at or past expert human level. On math and reasoning they've gotten quite strong. But on something like long-term memory, continual learning, they're close to zero. A model doesn't learn from working with you today in a way that persists to tomorrow unless you bolt on a retrieval scaffold, and retrieval isn't the same thing as actually consolidating new skills. Working memory, in the sense of robustly holding and manipulating state across a long task, is also much weaker than the headline numbers would suggest.

So when I see a benchmark result, the first question I ask is: which of these dimensions is this actually stressing? Something like MMLU or GPQA is mostly knowledge plus a bit of reasoning. Humanity's Last Exam is deliberately a knowledge-and-reasoning frontier test, and saturating it would tell you something about those dimensions and not much about others. If a model gets 90 percent on an expert-level exam, people extrapolate to "it's as capable as an expert," but an expert also remembers what happened last month, notices when they've made a mistake and corrects course, and doesn't fall apart on a trivially perturbed version of the question.

The second thing I'd say is that the gaps aren't just academic. The deficits in memory and in robust, grounded perception are precisely why these systems still can't be dropped into a job and left alone. So when I interpret benchmark performance, I'm less interested in the aggregate score and more interested in the profile. The profile tells you where the system will surprise you in a good way and where it'll fail in a way that an equivalently "smart" human never would. And I think if the field reported capabilities that way, as a profile across cognitive dimensions rather than a leaderboard number, a lot of the confusion about "is this AGI or not" would dissolve, because you'd see very clearly which boxes are filled in and which ones are still empty.

r001.rationale: The response says Humanity’s Last Exam measures knowledge and reasoning, but does not state that its mathematical ability need not bottleneck AI agency.

r002.rationale: It calls intelligence a “pretty lossy” single number and describes a profile across multiple cognitive dimensions.

r003.rationale: The response mentions visual processing but does not identify image classification as a facet of crystallized intelligence.

r004.rationale: It explains that saturating a knowledge-and-reasoning exam says little about other abilities, and connects memory and perception gaps to models’ inability to be left alone in a job.

r005.rationale: The response favors reporting a profile across dimensions, but does not propose human-level performance across those dimensions as a conception of AGI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to think of intelligence as multidimensional. A system might be very good at mathematical reasoning and much less good at understanding social situations or planning over a long horizon. So when we look at a benchmark, we should ask which capabilities it actually measures, rather than treating its score as a direct measurement of intelligence as a whole.

There can still be a general factor: performance across different cognitive tasks tends to be correlated. But that doesn’t mean the differences disappear. Two systems with the same average score could have very different strengths and weaknesses, and those differences might be precisely what matters for a particular application.

I’d also distinguish capability from how reliably that capability is expressed. Can the system solve a problem once, with the right prompt, or can it solve variations consistently? A benchmark gives us evidence about a particular slice of behavior. The challenge is figuring out how far that evidence generalizes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be careful about treating intelligence as a single number. There are different capabilities—reasoning, acquiring knowledge, planning—and a system can be very strong in one area and surprisingly weak in another. A benchmark samples some of those capabilities under particular conditions; it doesn’t give us a complete picture of the system.

So I’d look at the profile of performance. Can it generalize when you change the formulation of a problem? Can it apply what it knows in an unfamiliar setting? How reliable is it across different tasks? Those questions help distinguish getting a high score from having a capability that we can actually count on.

And then there’s a separate question about what the system does with those capabilities. Being more capable doesn’t automatically mean being more trustworthy. We need to evaluate those things separately.
